verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

Krishna agrees that the mind is restless, but he says that through practice and letting go, it can be trained. The mind is not meant to be forced into stillness. verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: After the story of two grieving brothers, Vasishtha tells Rama how worry feeds itself.
verse.sanskrit: चिन्तनेनैधते चिन्ता त्विन्धनेनेव पावकः । नश्यत्यचिन्ततेनैव विनेन्धनमिवानलः ॥
verse.line: Worry grows when you feed it thought, like fire with fuel. Starve it, and it dies down.
verse.translation: Worry grows by thinking, as fire grows with fuel; and it dies by not being thought, as fire dies without fuel.
verse.why: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.

prasang.title: Punya consoles his younger brother Pavana after their parents die
prasang.summary: Two brothers live with their parents by the Ganga. When their father and mother die, the elder, Punya, performs the rites calmly while the younger, Pavana, wanders the forest weeping. Punya gently helps him see that the bonds of 'mine' and 'not mine' are made in the mind. Vasishtha draws the lesson: worry grows when fed, and a full mind finds the world full.
prasang.story_hook: When their parents died, one brother quietly lit the funeral fires and the other ran weeping into the forest.
prasang.lesson: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha is speaking to Rama after the story of two brothers who lost their parents. The elder brother, Punya, saw that the younger, Pavana, was drowning in grief. Vasishtha tells Rama that worry grows by thinking, just as a fire grows with fuel, and it dies when you stop feeding it. The mind is not a solid thing. It is a habit of returning to the same thoughts. You can stop adding wood to the fire.
verse.for_you: Your mind is adding wood to a fire that has not happened. Today, when you catch yourself rehearsing a fear, do not argue with it. Simply stop adding the next thought. Let the flame use up what is already there and go out.

verse.line: "You are mine. Do not lose heart, do not tremble."
verse.translation: Having heard your ways, my trust and love are in you, yet I am afraid, seeing the cruelty of these times. It will only be well if you say it, or have it said, Ram: "Tulsi, you are mine. Do not lose heart, do not tremble."

prasang.title: Ram's grief and Lakshman's counsel
prasang.summary: Ram returns to an empty hut. He searches, questions trees and animals, breaks down and finally rages that he will destroy the world. Lakshman calms him: don't punish the whole world for one person's crime; trouble comes to everyone and passes.
prasang.story_hook: He came back to the hut calling her name, and no one answered.
prasang.lesson: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

verse.meaning: Lakshman speaks to Ram in the forest after Sita has been taken. Ram is shattered, raging that he will burn the world down. Lakshman tells him to take heart, that no living being is untouched by trouble. It strikes like fire and then passes. A steady voice in a broken room can stop grief from consuming everything. The idea is that loss is universal, and its heat, though fierce, is not permanent.
verse.for_you: Yesterday's verse named the grip. Today, sit with the heat of your own anxiety. Notice that it flares up, and that it will also pass. You do not need to solve the whole day right now.

story.summary: Six earnest seekers come to the sage Pippalada with questions. Instead of answering, he asks them to live with him for a year in discipline and faith, and only promises to answer what he actually knows.

script: You are pulled in every direction, and your mind is racing through what might go wrong before the day even begins.

Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is as hard to control as the wind. It is turbulent and stubborn, and he feels he cannot hold it steady. Krishna agrees that the mind is restless, but he says that through practice and letting go, it can be trained. Arjuna said:
चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम्, तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम्.
In plain words: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.

The mind is not meant to be forced into stillness. It is meant to be guided, again and again, until it learns where to settle. This is easier said than done, because the mind is strong and it resists. You cannot command it to stop by force. You train it by returning its attention, gently, every time it wanders. This is what practice means here. It is the letting go that trains it. Each time you stop fighting the thought and simply notice it, you are teaching the mind a new place to rest.

When you are with your children, your thoughts are already miles away. You do not have to empty your mind. You only need to set it down for one minute. Notice the thought, and then let your attention rest on the sound of their voice. That is the practice. That is the letting go.
Where is your mind resting right now?

depth.life: You are at the kitchen table after the kids have gone to bed. The house is quiet but your mind is not. It is running through the next day, what the clients might say, what the children might need. You are trying to rest, but your body is here and your thoughts are far away.
depth.points: Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless and strong, like the wind. It does not want to be controlled by force. The mind is not your enemy, but it does not listen to commands. It moves on its own, carrying your fears with it.
depth.practice: Sit for five minutes and watch your thoughts come and go. Do not try to catch them or push them away.
depth.question: What happens if you let the thoughts move without grabbing them?
